standard.title: Linear inequalities and simultaneous equations
standard.description: solve linear inequalities and simultaneous linear equations in 2 variables; interpret solutions graphically and communicate solutions in terms of the situation
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can find gradient, midpoint and distance between points on the Cartesian plane (AC9M9A03). They have not yet solved linear inequalities or simultaneous linear equations in 2 variables, nor interpreted solution regions graphically or communicated solutions in everyday context language.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students solve linear inequalities and simultaneous linear equations in 2 variables, interpret solutions graphically including solution regions, and communicate solutions in terms of the situation using appropriate context language.

nodes.label: Solving linear inequalities
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can solve a linear inequality in one variable algebraically and represent the solution on a number line.
nodes.minimum_width: Solve a one-variable linear inequality by isolating the variable; correctly reverse the inequality sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number; represent the solution on a number line.
nodes.typical_width: Solve linear inequalities in one variable involving multiple steps; handle all four inequality types; represent solutions on number lines; verify solutions by substitution.
wider: Investigate why multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the inequality direction using a concrete number line argument — building reasoning rather than rule-following
Explore compound inequalities (a < x < b) and their graphical representations, connecting to interval notation

response_modes.reason: The reversal rule for negative multiplication is a genuine misconception point — students who only see examples with positive divisors develop a fragile understanding. Multiple inequality types and both positive/negative operations are needed to stabilise the concept.

success_criteria: Student correctly reverses the inequality sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number
Student represents the solution set correctly on a number line, including open/closed circle distinction

nodes.label: Graphing linear inequalities in two variables
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can graph the solution region for a linear inequality in two variables in the Cartesian plane and verify a point's membership using substitution.
nodes.minimum_width: Graph the boundary line for a linear inequality in two variables; shade the correct half-plane; verify using a test point (e.g. (0,0)).
nodes.typical_width: Graph solution regions for linear inequalities in two variables using both solid and dashed boundary lines; verify regions using test points; represent constraints from practical problems as inequalities and graph their regions.
wider: Investigate the feasible region formed by two or more simultaneous linear inequalities — identify its vertices and discuss what the region represents in a practical context
Explore how graphical regions correspond to integer solution sets for budget or resource constraints, connecting continuous and discrete representations

response_modes.reason: Students frequently shade the wrong half-plane, especially when rearranging inequalities changes the orientation. The test-point method needs to be taught as a reliable verification strategy, not an afterthought.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The move from a single inequality's region to multiple overlapping regions is a genuinely rich extension — connecting to linear programming ideas, feasibility, and optimisation. Width investment here opens productive modelling territory for advancing students.
success_criteria: Student correctly identifies and shades the solution region for a given linear inequality in two variables
Student verifies whether a specified point satisfies the inequality using substitution

nodes.label: Solving simultaneous linear equations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can solve a pair of simultaneous linear equations in 2 variables using algebraic methods (substitution or elimination).
nodes.minimum_width: Solve a pair of simultaneous linear equations using either substitution or elimination; verify the solution by substituting into both equations.
nodes.typical_width: Solve simultaneous linear equations using substitution, elimination and graphical methods; choose the most efficient method for a given pair; verify solutions; recognise that parallel lines have no solution and coincident lines have infinitely many.
wider: Investigate the strategies inherent in First Nations Australian children's instructive games (e.g. Weme from the Warlpiri Peoples) and their connection to solving simultaneous equations
Explore systems where elimination requires scaling one or both equations and discuss why the solution is preserved under these operations

response_modes.reason: Sign errors in elimination (especially subtracting equations) are a persistent source of mistakes. Fluency with both substitution and elimination methods requires deliberate practice before contextualised application.

success_criteria: Student correctly solves a pair of simultaneous linear equations and verifies the solution in both equations
Student can apply both substitution and elimination, selecting an appropriate method for the given pair
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot solve simultaneous equations reliably cannot proceed to N4 — contextual formulation and interpretation both require a correct algebraic solution to reason about.

nodes.label: Interpreting and communicating solutions in context
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can formulate a practical problem as simultaneous equations or inequalities, solve it, and communicate the solution in plain language appropriate to the context.
nodes.minimum_width: Define variables for a context problem, write simultaneous equations, solve, and state the answer in everyday terms relevant to the situation.
nodes.typical_width: Formulate, solve and interpret simultaneous equations and linear inequalities across multiple practical contexts (pricing comparisons, budget constraints, break-even analysis); use appropriate context language ('break-even point', 'feasible combinations'); interpret graphical solutions within the situation; identify integer constraints where relevant.
wider: Investigate how simultaneous equations model real supply-and-demand or profit-and-loss scenarios; evaluate the assumptions the model makes and discuss when the model breaks down
Explore First Nations Australian children's instructive games as contexts for strategy and constraint analysis, investigating connections to mathematical solution structures

response_modes.reason: Translation between contextual language and algebraic formulation is a genuine hinge — students who can solve equations but struggle to set them up from context have an incomplete understanding. Multiple context types (pricing, budget, resource allocation) build the translation skill.

This node integrates all prior procedural work (solving inequalities, solving simultaneous equations, graphing regions) into the full problem-solving cycle. Formulation, solution and interpretation must operate together.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The contextualised application is where mathematical reasoning becomes genuinely purposeful — rich contexts (break-even analysis, resource constraints, community budget problems) give advancing students meaningful modelling work at the year band.
success_criteria: Student correctly defines variables and formulates simultaneous equations or inequalities from a described context
Student states the solution in terms of the original context using appropriate everyday language
Student identifies whether the solution makes sense within the context's constraints (e.g. integer values, non-negative quantities)
